transcript: Eurydice by Sarah Ruhl has been around for a while and is frequently produced all over the country, but I was lucky enough to experience it for the first time with Maya Hawke making a meal out of the title role. This melancholic, strange, and whimsically poetic take on the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice is largely about memory and relationships, and much of the play illustrates characters trying to find ways to communicate with each other. Language and music are simultaneously in harmony and at odds with one another, and love is conveyed in tender but peculiar ways — the reading of Shakespeare, a symphony for twelve instruments, a room made of string. In the world of this play, things kind of make no sense but are taken to make perfect sense, and this production makes the most out of a small space in its design and direction to create some imaginatively striking moments. The performances certainly help as well, with Maya Hawke delivering a youthful but assured portrayal of Eurydice, accompanied by a wonderful pair in Brian d’Arcy James and Caleb Eberhardt as Father and Orpheus. This play is just as much about Eurydice and her father as it is about Eurydice and Orpheus, and there were multiple scenes between Maya and Brian that broke my heart. To then learn that Sarah Ruhl dedicated the play to her father who passed away when she was in college makes it all the more devastating, and I think the confusing nature of grief and loss that permeates through this piece is what makes it so timeless. I am not surprised that this play is produced all the time, all over the place. This production of Eurydice is running at Signature through June 22nd. With that, another program for my collection.
